name: Ahab
title: King of the Northern Kingdom of Israel and Worshiper of Baal
summary: Ahab, son of Omri, reigned as the seventh king over the Northern Kingdom of Israel for about 22 years (c. 874–853 BC). By marrying Jezebel, a Phoenician princess and daughter of King Ethbaal of Sidon, he paved the way for the systematic introduction of Baal worship into the kingdom and had a temple to Baal built in the capital city of Samaria. Scripture states that he provoked the Lord's anger more than any of Israel's kings before him (1 Kings 16:33). Despite the prophet Elijah's powerful confrontation with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, where the Lord's fire fell and the people confessed the God of Israel, Ahab held fast to idolatry. At the same time, he was a politically and militarily capable ruler who carried out extensive building projects – including the famous ivory palace in Samaria – and met Assyria's expansion by fielding the largest chariot force in an international coalition at Qarqar in 853 BC. The incident with Naboth's vineyard reveals the moral corruption of his reign: Jezebel arranged the murder of the innocent Naboth through false accusations, and Elijah proclaimed God's judgment over Ahab's entire dynastic line. When the king humbled himself before the Lord, the fulfillment was postponed to the next generation – a striking testimony that God's mercy reaches even the most stubborn. Ahab fell in battle at Ramoth Gilead, struck by what seemed like a random arrow, just as the prophet Micaiah had predicted, and dogs licked his blood by the pool of Samaria in fulfillment of God's word.

keyEvents.title: Married Jezebel and Introduced Baal Worship
keyEvents.description: Ahab took the Phoenician princess Jezebel as his wife and built a temple to Baal in Samaria. Scripture states that he did more to provoke the Lord's anger than all the kings of Israel before him.

keyEvents.title: The Confrontation with Elijah on Mount Carmel
keyEvents.description: Elijah challenged Ahab and the 450 prophets of Ba'al to a sacrifice test on Mount Carmel. The Lord answered with fire from heaven and demonstrated His sovereignty over Ba'al. The people fell down and confessed that the Lord is God.

keyEvents.title: The Wars Against Aram and Ben-Hadad
keyEvents.description: Ahab fought against King Ben-Hadad of Aram and won twice with God's help, but he let Ben-Hadad go free in defiance of God's will. A prophet declared judgment on Ahab because he had released a man whom God had devoted to destruction.

keyEvents.title: Naboth's Vineyard
keyEvents.description: Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard in Jezreel, and Jezebel arranged for Naboth's execution through false witnesses and accusations. The prophet Elijah proclaimed God's judgment on Ahab and his entire household. When Ahab humbled himself, God postponed the full judgment to the next generation.

keyEvents.title: The Death of Ahab at Ramoth-Gilead
keyEvents.description: Ahab went to war against Ramoth in Gilead together with Jehoshaphat of Judah, despite the prophet Micaiah's warning of defeat. Disguised as a common soldier, he was struck by a random arrow and died at sunset. Dogs licked his blood at the pool in Samaria, fulfilling God's word.

versions.summary: Ahab was king over the Northern Kingdom of Israel for 22 years and married the Phoenician princess Jezebel. He did more evil than all the kings before him by introducing Baal worship. Despite the mighty deeds of the prophet Elijah, Ahab remained in idolatry. He died in battle as prophesied.
versions.title: Israel's Most Evil King
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Israel's most wicked king' is dramatic, but biblically quite accurate (1 Kings 16:30,33; 21:25). Still, it may be more precise to say 'Israel's seventh king of the Northern Kingdom' or similar, but given 1 Kings 21:25 which explicitly states that no one was like Ahab, the title can be defended. A slightly more balanced title could include his role as king over the Northern Kingdom.; [critical] Ahab's father was Omri, king of Israel (1 Kings 16:28-29). This is missing and is an important family relationship error.; [major] Ahab had several well-known children, including Ahaziah (1 Kings 22:40,52) and Joram (2 Kings 3:1), who both became kings of Israel, as well as his daughter Athaliah (2 Kings 8:18,26). These should be included.; [minor] Ahab was also a military leader and builder (1 Kings 22:39 mentions the ivory palace). He can also be described as an idolater. The roles should be expanded somewhat.; [minor] Ahab's reign is usually dated to about 874–853 BC. Lifespan 'about 919-852 BC' gives a birth year that is very uncertain. 852 BC is close to the usual death year (853 BC), but it can be adjusted slightly to align with common chronology.; [minor] The summary is good, but could mention that Ahab was the son of Omri, and that he was a politically and militarily powerful king despite his spiritual failure. It could also note that he showed humility after the incident involving Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21:27-29), which is an important theological point.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Ahab is one of the most archaeologically documented kings in the Old Testament, mentioned in the Kurkh Monolith from Assyrian king Shalmaneser III, and on the Mesha Stele. Footnotes about this should be added.; [minor] The war against Syria/Aram and the alliance with Ben-Hadad (1 Kings 20) is an important event that is missing. Ahab's military activities were significant.

versions.summary: Ahab, son of Omri, was the seventh king over the northern kingdom of Israel and reigned for 22 years (c. 874–853 B.C.). He married the Phoenician princess Jezebel and systematically introduced Baal worship in Israel, making him the most notorious king in the history of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 21:25). Despite the mighty deeds of the prophet Elijah and the confrontation on Mount Carmel, Ahab largely remained in idolatry. Ahab was also a politically and militarily powerful ruler with significant building projects. After he allowed Jezebel to arrange the murder of Naboth, he humbled himself before God, and the judgment was postponed to the next generation. He fell in battle at Ramoth in Gilead, struck by a random arrow, as the prophet Micaiah had predicted.
versions.title: King of the Northern Kingdom of Israel and Worshiper of Baal
versions.reason: [minor] Ahab was not only a political and military leader but also a central figure in the biblical narrative about idolatry. A role such as 'idolater' or similar could clarify this, especially since the title already mentions Baal worship.; [minor] Athaliah is traditionally identified as the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, but 2 Kings 8:26 calls her 'granddaughter of Omri'. Some scholars debate whether she was Ahab's daughter or Omri's daughter/granddaughter. It may be worth noting this uncertainty, but the traditional interpretation (daughter of Ahab) is most widespread and acceptable.

versions.summary: Ahab, son of Omri, reigned as the seventh king over the Northern Kingdom of Israel for about 22 years (c. 874–853 BC). Through his marriage to Jezebel, a Phoenician princess from Sidon, he systematically introduced Baal worship into Israel and had a temple built for Baal in the capital city of Samaria. Scripture describes him as the king who provoked the Lord's anger more than any of his predecessors (1 Kings 16:33). Despite Elijah's powerful confrontation with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, Ahab did not permanently turn away from idolatry. Politically and militarily, however, he was one of the Northern Kingdom's most powerful rulers: he carried out major building projects, including the ivory palace in Samaria, and contributed a significant army to the international coalition against Assyria at Qarqar. After the injustice toward Nabot—where Jezebel arranged his murder to secure his vineyard—Elijah proclaimed God's judgment over Ahab's entire dynastic line. When Ahab humbled himself before the Lord, the full judgment was postponed to the next generation, a testimony to God's mercy even toward the most stubborn. Ahab met his death in the battle at Ramoth Gilead, struck by what appeared to be a random arrow, fulfilling the words of the prophet Micaiah.
versions.title: King of the Northern Kingdom of Israel and Worshiper of Baal
versions.reason: [minor] The word 'dynastic' should be 'dynastical' (adjective in definite form: 'the entire dynastical line of Ahab').; [minor] The number of Ba'al prophets was 450 plus 400 Asherah prophets (1 Kings 18:19). The description mentions only the 450 Ba'al prophets, which is correct for the sacrifice test itself, but it could have been useful to note that the 400 Asherah prophets were also summoned.; [minor] Athaliah is identified in 2 Kings 8:26 as 'daughter of Omri', which may mean granddaughter rather than direct daughter of Ahab. Many scholars believe she was Ahab's daughter, but the relationship is disputed. It may be worth noting this uncertainty.

footnotes.text: Ahab is mentioned on the Assyrian Kurkh Monolith (c. 853 BC), which describes the Battle of Qarqar. There, Ahab is referred to as 'Ahab of Israel' (A-ha-ab-bu Sir-ila-a-a) and he contributed 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers—the largest chariot force in the coalition against Shalmaneser III.

The Omride dynasty is also mentioned on the Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), where King Mesha of Moab describes how he freed himself from Israel's dominance under Omri and his 'son' (likely including Ahab).
The name Ahab (Hebrew: אַחְאָב, 'Aḥ'av) means 'father's brother' or 'brother to the father,' a common Semitic naming pattern expressing kinship and family loyalty.

1 Kings 21:25–26 gives a summary judgment on Ahab as unique in his wickedness, but the text in 1 Kings 21:27–29 also shows that his humility led God to postpone the judgment to the next generation—an important theological point about repentance and God's mercy.
Ahab's ivory palace (1 Kings 22:39) has been confirmed archaeologically. Excavations in Samaria have uncovered hundreds of ivory carvings from the 8th century BC, matching the biblical description.

In rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 102b), Ahab's character is discussed with surprising nuance. Some rabbis credited him with merit for honoring the Torah, and his humility in 1 Kings 21 is taken as evidence that repentance is possible even for the most wicked rulers.

Ahab's alliance with King Jehoshaphat of Judah through the marriage between Athaliah and Joram of Judah represented a significant political pact between the two kingdoms, but it had serious consequences when Athaliah later seized power in Jerusalem and nearly wiped out David's royal line (2 Kings 11).

Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31). The Phoenician historian Menander of Tyre, quoted by Josephus, identifies Ethbaal as a priest of Astarte who seized power through a coup—a background that may shed light on Jezebel's religious influence over Ahab.
